claims.claim: Keeley says a small detail in one volume of The Book of the New Sun frequently presages a large revelation in a later one.
claims.quote: a small detail in one book frequently presages a large revelation

claims.claim: Novelist Michael Swanwick rates Wolfe's prose as good as prose gets, in a beginners' guide first printed in F&SF in 2007.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016
claims.quote: his prose is as good as prose gets

claims.claim: Swanwick says Wolfe is notorious for never explaining his stories, so no reader can tell where interpretation stops.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016
claims.quote: Gene Wolfe is notorious for never explaining his stories

claims.claim: Swanwick's first rule for reading Wolfe is to look for hidden implications.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016

claims.claim: Swanwick's second rule for reading Wolfe is to pay serious attention to the obvious, citing Poe's purloined letter.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016
claims.quote: Remember Poe’s purloined letter, and pay serious attention to the obvious.

claims.claim: Swanwick tells the reader of the story 'Memorare' to look up the prayer of that name to see what Wolfe left out of it.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016
claims.quote: look up the prayer to see what Wolfe left out

claims.claim: Swanwick warns that a Wolfe story's surface meaning cannot be ignored merely because the story also has deeper levels.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016
claims.quote: simply because a story has deeper levels, its surface meaning can be
claims.page: essay, after the Solar Labyrinth section

claims.claim: Swanwick says Wolfe always leaves room in his work for more than one interpretation.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016
claims.quote: Wolfe always leaves room for multiple interpretations in his work.

claims.claim: Swanwick points to the engineering detail of the suits and cenotaphs in 'Memorare' as craftsmanship on the story's surface.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016
claims.quote: Note the careful engineering of the suits and cenotaphs.

claims.claim: Wolfe, quoted by Swanwick from his short essay 'What I Know About Writing (in no particular order)', wrote that an interesting work of art comes close to saying the opposite of what it says.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, 'What I Know About Writing (in no particular order)', quoted by Michael Swanwick
claims.quote: Almost any interesting work of art comes close to saying the opposite

claims.claim: Swanwick says annotation pays off on Wolfe because he puts more into his works than almost any other writer.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Explicated Gene Wolfe', Flogging Babel, 2009
claims.quote: so much more into his works than almost any other writer

claims.claim: Swanwick likens Wolfe's buried details to programmers' Easter eggs, not needed for enjoying the story.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Explicated Gene Wolfe', Flogging Babel, 2009
claims.quote: not necessary for your enjoyment of the experience

claims.claim: John Barach reports Wolfe's own statement that he gives a clue only once.
claims.source: John Barach, 'How to Read Gene Wolfe', Kata Iwannhn blog, 2007
claims.quote: he gives a clue only once

claims.claim: Ada Palmer's foreword to the Tor Essentials Shadow & Claw, quoted by Livia J. Elliot, says reading for world-building requires retaining information without context.
claims.source: Ada Palmer, foreword to Shadow & Claw (Tor Essentials), quoted by Livia J. Elliot, 2024
claims.quote: Reading for world-building requires retaining information without context

claims.claim: Author Livia J. Elliot says Wolfe often gives information about the world without context.
claims.source: Livia J. Elliot, 'The Puzzle Left Behind', Books Undone ep. 010 transcript, 2024
claims.quote: give information about the world without context
